guide.title: Nob Hill, San Francisco: Grace Cathedral, the cable car powerhouse and the Flood Mansion
guide.intro: Nob Hill is a hill in central San Francisco, and the California Street cable car line runs along California Street across it. In 1876 Charles Crocker, one of the Big Four builders of the transcontinental railroad, built a mansion on the block where the cathedral nave now stands. The hill took its name from "nabob". Grace Cathedral holds that block now, and its close occupies a 2.5-acre city block. The Cable Car Museum stands in the working Washington-Mason powerhouse and carbarn, where admission is free. The Flood Mansion at 1000 California Street houses the Pacific-Union Club, which is private. Huntington Park fills the block bounded by Taylor, Sacramento, California and Cushman Streets. The Fairmont, the InterContinental Mark Hopkins and the Stanford Court all take addresses on the hill's own streets, and Top of the Mark is the lounge on the top floor of the Mark Hopkins.

sections.heading: The cathedral block, the club and the powerhouse
sections.body:
Charles Crocker was buying up the block that Grace Cathedral now holds in 1874, and Nicholas Yung, a German undertaker, refused to sell to him. The fence that went up around Yung's property remained until 1904, and Yung himself moved his house away long before that. The William H. Crockers later gave the block to the Episcopal Diocese of California. A pro-cathedral went up in 1907, the cornerstone was laid in 1910, the present cathedral was begun in 1927 and the largely completed building was consecrated in 1964.

The other two anchors on the hill were built for money of the same generation and are used for very different things today. The Flood Mansion at 1000 California Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 64, designated in 1974, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 13 November 1966 as the James C. Flood Mansion, reference number 66000230. It houses the Pacific-Union Club, which is private, so there are no visiting hours. The Cable Car Barn And Power House at 1201 Mason Street is a working powerhouse with the Cable Car Museum inside it, and it is San Francisco Landmark No. 43, designated in 1971.

South of the hill's own streets runs a district nobody needs a ticket for. The Lower Nob Hill Apartment Hotel Historic District was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 31 July 1991, reference number 91000957, with a period of significance from 1906 to 1940. SF Planning describes it as a dense area primarily comprised of 3- to 7-story multi-unit residential buildings, most of them built between 1906 and 1925, leading to a stylistically consistent district, and gives its extent as roughly 590 to 1209 Bush, 680 to 1156 Sutter and 600 to 1099 Post Streets.

One piece of street furniture is worth looking down for. Circular brick rings are set into the roadway at Taylor and Clay, at Powell and Bush, at Mason and California, and at Jones and Jackson. They are the covers of cisterns belonging to the city's Auxiliary Water Supply System, and there are more of them in the streets beyond.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The California Street cable car line runs along California Street across Nob Hill. SFMTA gives three lines in all: two start at Powell and Market and continue to the Fisherman's Wharf area, and one starts at California and Market and continues to Van Ness Avenue. SFMTA also states that to board cable cars at Powell & Market, Bay & Taylor and Hyde & Beach Streets you must purchase your fare in advance, and that this applies from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily. No source states a fare, so none is given here.

Steer by street addresses. On California Street: Grace Cathedral at 1100, The Masonic at 1111, the Flood Mansion at 1000, the InterContinental Mark Hopkins and Top of the Mark at 999, the Stanford Court at 905. On Mason Street: the Fairmont at 950, the Cable Car Museum at 1201. On Taylor Street: Huntington Park at 1000, the Glazer-Keating House at 1110, Nob Hill Cafe at 1152. Elsewhere: the Chambord Apartments at 1298 Sacramento Street, the Dennis T. Sullivan Memorial Home at 870 Bush Street, Woh Hei Yuen Park at 922 Jackson Street and Our Lady of Guadalupe Church at 906 Broadway.

Two buildings answer to two addresses each, which defeats map software as well as visitors. Grace Cathedral's own footer gives 1100 California Street, while the city's Article 10 record gives 1051 to 1055 Taylor Street; both are the parcel APN 0246001, one property with two street frontages. The Cable Car Museum gives 1201 Mason Street on its own site, while the National Park Service addresses the cable car record, reference number 66000233, to 1390 Washington Street. Same building, other corner.

sections.heading: Hours, admission and where to eat
sections.body:
Grace Cathedral opens Monday to Saturday 10am to 5pm and Sundays 1pm to 5pm. Its indoor labyrinth is open during cathedral visitor hours and its outdoor labyrinth is open at all hours. Admission to the Cable Car Museum is free; the museum's own site gives its opening days in two ways that do not agree, so no days are given here. No source states opening hours for Huntington Park or for Woh Hei Yuen Park, so none are given here. The Pacific-Union Club is private and the Chambord Apartments and the Glazer-Keating House are lived in, so none of the three has visiting hours.

For food and drink the hill publishes two sets of hours and withholds a third. Top of the Mark, the cocktail lounge on the top floor of the InterContinental Mark Hopkins at 999 California Street, opens Sunday to Thursday 4pm to 11pm and Friday and Saturday 3pm to 12.30am, with the kitchen taking its last order at 9.30pm. Nob Hill Cafe at 1152 Taylor Street serves dinner Sunday to Thursday 5pm to 9pm and Friday and Saturday 5pm to 10pm, and brunch Saturday and Sunday 11am to 3pm; it takes no reservations and serves walk-ins only. The Fairmont names Tonga Room & Hurricane Bar, Laurel Court Restaurant & Bar and Cirque Bar among its dining rooms, along with Timeless Tea, Bin 415 and in-room dining. No source states their hours, so none are given here.

The Masonic at 1111 California Street is a concert hall operated by Live Nation, and its programme rather than an opening time is what governs a visit. No source states a capacity for it.

faq.question: Is Grace Cathedral open to visitors, and what are the labyrinths?
faq.answer: The cathedral's own site gives Monday to Saturday 10am to 5pm and Sundays 1pm to 5pm. Grace Cathedral has an indoor and an outdoor labyrinth, both in the Chartres pattern. The indoor labyrinth is open during cathedral visitor hours and the outdoor labyrinth is open at all hours. Canon Lauren Artress introduced the labyrinth in 1991. The building is 329 feet (100m) long and 162 feet (49m) wide at the transepts, and the nave vaulting rises to 91 feet (27m).

faq.question: Can you go inside the Flood Mansion?
faq.answer: No. The Flood Mansion at 1000 California Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 64, designated in 1974, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 13 November 1966 as the James C. Flood Mansion, reference number 66000230. It is a National Historic Landmark. The building houses the Pacific-Union Club, which is private, so there are no visiting hours. SF Planning records the building as built in 1911.

faq.question: What does the Cable Car Museum cost, and when is it open?
faq.answer: Admission is free. The museum's own site gives its opening days in two ways that do not agree, so no days are given here. It is at 1201 Mason Street, inside what its own site calls the Washington-Mason powerhouse and carbarn on Nob Hill, and it is run by the Friends of the Cable Car Museum, a nonprofit organization dedicated to the preservation of cable car history.

faq.question: Which cable car line serves Nob Hill?
faq.answer: The California Street cable car line runs along California Street across Nob Hill. SFMTA gives three lines in all: two start at Powell and Market and continue to the Fisherman's Wharf area, and one starts at California and Market and continues to Van Ness Avenue. SFMTA states that to board cable cars at Powell & Market, Bay & Taylor and Hyde & Beach Streets you must purchase your fare in advance, applying from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily.

faq.question: Where can you eat and drink without a reservation?
faq.answer: Nob Hill Cafe at 1152 Taylor Street takes no reservations and serves walk-ins only, with dinner Sunday to Thursday 5pm to 9pm and Friday and Saturday 5pm to 10pm and brunch Saturday and Sunday 11am to 3pm. Top of the Mark at 999 California Street opens Sunday to Thursday 4pm to 11pm and Friday and Saturday 3pm to 12.30am, with a last kitchen order at 9.30pm. The Fairmont names Tonga Room & Hurricane Bar, Laurel Court Restaurant & Bar and Cirque Bar among its dining rooms, but no source states their hours.

faq.question: How did Nob Hill get its name?
faq.answer: Grace Cathedral's own history records that in 1876 Charles Crocker, one of the Big Four builders of the transcontinental railroad, built a mansion on the block where the cathedral nave now stands, and that the hill took its name from "nabob". The same account records that Nicholas Yung, a German undertaker, refused to sell to Crocker when Crocker was buying up the block in 1874, and that the fence raised around Yung's property remained until 1904.

places.name: Grace Cathedral
places.summary: Grace Cathedral is the cathedral of the Episcopal Diocese of California, at 1100 California Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 170, designated in 1984, and the cathedral's own architecture page records that the designation covers the bordering Crocker walls and Diocesan House as well as the church. It opens Monday to Saturday 10am to 5pm and Sundays 1pm to 5pm. The cathedral is 329 feet (100m) long and 162 feet (49m) wide at the transepts, and the nave vaulting rises to 91 feet (27m). It faces 9 degrees 15 minutes south of due west, parallel to adjacent California Street, and the sanctuary floor around the High Altar steps stands 299.5 feet (91.4m) above mean sea level.
places.history:
Grace Chapel was built in the 1849 Gold Rush on Powell Street near Jackson, and a brick Gothic church at California and Stockton followed in 1862; it burned in 1906. The William H. Crockers gave their block to the diocese, a pro-cathedral was built in 1907 and the cornerstone was laid in 1910. George Bodley prepared plans; his death led to a design by his partner Cecil Hare, and Hare's local agent Lewis Hobart became official architect and redesigned the building. The Founders Crypt served from 1914 to 1930. The present cathedral was begun in 1927, the Chapel of Grace opened in 1930, and by 1934 the two-thirds-built cathedral was opened for use. The north tower went up between 1936 and 1943, work resumed in 1960 and the largely completed cathedral was consecrated in 1964. The Cathedral School for Boys was begun in 1956 and the close was finished in 1995; it occupies a 2.5-acre city block.

Hobart chose French Gothic, on a cruciform plan with twin towers, a central fleche and a polygonal apse, taking Amiens, Notre-Dame, Beauvais and Chartres as influences. The wide nave, narrow piers and absent triforium follow Aragonese Gothic and Palma, Majorca; the nave clerestory is English; the Chapel of Grace follows the Sainte-Chapelle. The fabric is raw concrete and steel because the 1906 earthquake made structural strength necessary: riveted steel lattices, beams and reinforcing bar from 1927 to 1943, clustered steel bar and beams from 1960 to 1964, and Guastavino acoustic tile in the vaulting.

Grace Cathedral has an indoor and an outdoor labyrinth, both in the Chartres pattern. The indoor labyrinth is open during cathedral visitor hours and the outdoor labyrinth is open at all hours. Canon Lauren Artress introduced the labyrinth in 1991. The AIDS Interfaith Memorial Chapel occupies the north tower lobby, set aside in 1995. Its first major furnishing was a casting of "The Life of Christ", a triptych altarpiece Keith Haring made in 1990. The cathedral records that the casting was obtained with the help of Haring's friend Yoko Ono and the local activist Frank Malifrando, and that it is shaped like a Russian icon.

places.name: Cable Car Museum
places.summary: The Cable Car Museum is at 1201 Mason Street, inside what its own site calls the Washington-Mason powerhouse and carbarn on Nob Hill, so the winding machinery a visitor looks at is the machinery still hauling the cars up the street outside. It is run by the Friends of the Cable Car Museum, a nonprofit organization dedicated to the preservation of cable car history. Admission is free. The museum's own site gives its opening days in two ways that do not agree, so no days are given here.
places.history: The building is San Francisco Landmark No. 43, designated in 1971 under the name Cable Car Barn And Power House, and SF Planning records the parcel as built in 1900. The cable cars were listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 15 October 1966 as San Francisco Cable Cars, reference number 66000233, and are a National Historic Landmark; the National Park Service addresses that record to 1390 Washington Street, which is the same building off its other frontage.

places.name: Flood Mansion and the Pacific-Union Club
places.summary: The Flood Mansion at 1000 California Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 64, designated in 1974, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 13 November 1966 as the James C. Flood Mansion, reference number 66000230. It is a National Historic Landmark. The building houses the Pacific-Union Club, which is private, so there are no visiting hours.
places.history: SF Planning records the building as built in 1911, on parcel APN 0245001. The National Park Service holds its address as California and Mason Streets. No source states the name of its architect.

places.name: The Fairmont San Francisco
places.summary: The Fairmont San Francisco is at 950 Mason Street. The hotel names Tonga Room & Hurricane Bar, Laurel Court Restaurant & Bar and Cirque Bar among its dining rooms. No source states their hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The hotel is San Francisco Landmark No. 185, designated in 1987, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 17 April 2002, reference number 02000373. Its own site names Timeless Tea, Bin 415 and in-room dining alongside its three bars and restaurants.

places.name: InterContinental Mark Hopkins
places.summary: The InterContinental Mark Hopkins occupies the corner of California and Mason Streets, and answers to two addresses: the city's Article 10 record gives 850 Mason Street and SF Planning's parcel record for the same building gives 999 California Street. Top of the Mark is the cocktail lounge on its top floor.
places.history: The building is San Francisco Landmark No. 184, designated in 1987 under the name Mark Hopkins Hotel. SF Planning records the building as built in 1926.

places.name: Top of the Mark
places.summary: Top of the Mark is a cocktail lounge on the top floor of the InterContinental Mark Hopkins at 999 California Street. It opens Sunday to Thursday 4pm to 11pm and Friday and Saturday 3pm to 12.30am. The kitchen takes its last order at 9.30pm.
places.history: SF Planning records the building it sits on top of as built in 1926.

places.name: Huntington Park
places.summary: Huntington Park occupies the block bounded by Taylor, Sacramento, California and Cushman Streets. San Francisco Recreation and Parks records it as Collis P Huntington Park, a civic plaza or square of 1.29 acres. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The city's Civic Art Collection catalogues two sculptures in the park. The Fountain of the Tortoises, by Taddeo, is a marble and bronze work of 1900, accession 1954.18, credited as the gift of Mrs William H. Crocker and standing in the centre of the park. Dancing Sprites, by Henri Leon Greber, is a bronze of about 1942, 45 inches high and 4 feet in diameter, accession 1942.1, credited as the gift of Mrs James L. Flood. Recreation and Parks gives the park a perimeter of 953.18 feet and an area of 56,460.97 square feet.

places.name: Chambord Apartments
places.summary: The Chambord Apartments stand at 1298 Sacramento Street. The building is San Francisco Landmark No. 106, designated in 1979, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 20 September 1984, reference number 84001184. It is lived in, so there are no visiting hours and it is seen from the pavement.
places.history: SF Planning records the building as built in 1922, on parcel APN 0221125. No source states the name of its architect.

places.name: Glazer-Keating House
places.summary: The Glazer-Keating House at 1110 Taylor Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 251, designated in 2005. It is a private house, so there are no visiting hours.
places.history: SF Planning records the house as built in 1906, on parcel APN 0222018. No source states the name of its architect.

places.name: The Masonic
places.summary: The Masonic is a concert hall at 1111 California Street, operated by Live Nation. SF Planning records the building as built in 1956.
places.history: No source states an architect, an opening date or a seating capacity for the hall, so none is given here.

places.name: Nob Hill Cafe
places.summary: Nob Hill Cafe is at 1152 Taylor Street and serves home-cooked Italian food. Dinner is Sunday to Thursday 5pm to 9pm and Friday and Saturday 5pm to 10pm; brunch is Saturday and Sunday 11am to 3pm. It takes no reservations.
places.history: The restaurant is at 1152 Taylor Street. No source states a history of the business, so none is given here.

places.name: Stanford Court
places.summary: The Stanford Court is at 905 California Street. SF Planning records the building as built in 1971.
places.history: The parcel record covers 901 to 905 California Street. No source states a history of the building, so none is given here.

places.name: California Street cable car line
places.summary: The California Street cable car line runs along California Street across Nob Hill. SFMTA gives three lines in all: two start at Powell and Market and continue to the Fisherman's Wharf area, and one starts at California and Market and continues to Van Ness Avenue.
places.history: The cable cars were listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 15 October 1966 as San Francisco Cable Cars, reference number 66000233, and are a National Historic Landmark. SFMTA states that to board cable cars at Powell & Market, Bay & Taylor and Hyde & Beach Streets you must purchase your fare in advance, and that this applies from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily. No source states a fare, so none is given here.

places.name: Dennis T. Sullivan Memorial Home
places.summary: The Dennis T. Sullivan Memorial Home at 870 Bush Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 42, designated in 1971. It is the Fire Chief's residence and carries M. Earl Cummings' bronze plaque to Dennis T. Sullivan (1852-1906), dated 1921, accession 1921.1 in the Civic Art Collection.
places.history: The Civic Art Collection records the plaque as 88 by 41.5 by 5.5 inches. The house is a residence, so there are no visiting hours and the plaque is read from the pavement.

places.name: Woh Hei Yuen Park
places.summary: Woh Hei Yuen Park is at 922 Jackson Street. San Francisco Recreation and Parks records it as a park of 0.356 acres. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the park, so none is given here.

places.name: Our Lady of Guadalupe Church
places.summary: The church of Our Lady of Guadalupe at 906 Broadway is San Francisco Landmark No. 204, designated in 1993. No source states opening or service times for it, so none are given here, and the building is seen from the pavement.
places.history: SF Planning holds the property as parcel APN 0149009. No source states the name of its architect or the date of its building.
